questions.question: ___ tries to ensure meeting of specification time to time, whereas ___ rather measures the meeting of intended purpose.
questions.explanation: Monitoring is the continuous, periodic tracking of whether a project is meeting its specifications, milestones and targets 'time to time' (ongoing check-ins), while evaluation is the periodic, deeper assessment of whether the project actually achieved its intended purpose/objectives. This is the standard textbook distinction (syllabus subtopic 'Difference between monitoring and evaluation'). Reversing the order (a) inverts the definitions, (b) substitutes the wrong first term, and (d) substitutes unrelated job roles for the two M&E concepts being contrasted.

questions.question: Which statement is false regarding Monitoring?

options.A: Process of routinely gathering information on all aspects of the project

questions.explanation: Monitoring is continuous, routine tracking of inputs, activities and outputs so problems can be spotted early and resources used well; judging whether the programme actually achieved its objectives is the job of evaluation. Confusing the two is the standard trap in monitoring and evaluation questions.

questions.question: In certain e-Governance project, the Evaluation measures:
questions.explanation: In the results chain, monitoring tracks outputs while evaluation assesses outcomes - the changes actually produced for users by the delivered services. Output is what monitoring measures, and success/failure is a verdict rather than a measurement category.

questions.question: An evaluation carried out while a project is still being implemented, whose findings are meant to correct the design and delivery of the project in progress, is best described as:
questions.explanation: A formative evaluation is deliberately timed so that its conclusions can still change what the project does — it asks whether implementation is on the right track and what should be adjusted. Summative, terminal and ex-post evaluations all judge a project after the fact and produce lessons for the next project rather than corrections to this one.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes monitoring from evaluation in an e-governance project?

options.A: Monitoring is always carried out by an external agency, whereas evaluation is always internal to the department
options.B: Monitoring assesses relevance and long-term results, while evaluation records physical and financial progress
options.C: Monitoring is the continuous tracking of inputs, activities and outputs against the plan, while evaluation is a periodic and deeper judgement of whether the project is relevant, efficient and achieving its intended results
options.D: Monitoring and evaluation are two names for the same periodic review exercise

questions.explanation: Monitoring is routine and internal to implementation — it answers 'are we doing what we said we would, on time and on budget'; evaluation is episodic and more analytical, asking whether the effort was worth making and whether it worked. Option B inverts the two, which is the most common confusion, and the external-versus-internal split is a matter of who commissions the exercise, not what separates the two functions.

questions.sub: Approach for development of a Monitoring and Evaluation Framework
questions.question: In an M&E framework, what must be specified for each indicator in addition to how the indicator is defined and calculated?

options.A: The name of the vendor that will supply the underlying data
options.B: The budget head from which the indicator is funded
options.C: The penalty applicable if the indicator is not met
options.D: Its data source, the method and frequency of collection, and the officer or unit responsible for reporting it

questions.explanation: An indicator only becomes operational when the framework says where the number comes from, how often it is captured and who is accountable for producing it — otherwise it is an intention rather than a measurement. Penalties belong to the contract with the implementing vendor and are a separate instrument from the department's own monitoring framework.

questions.sub: Approach for development of a Monitoring and Evaluation Framework
questions.question: Why should the M&E framework for an e-governance project be designed and put in place before implementation starts, rather than after the system goes live?

options.A: Because the baseline values of the indicators can only be captured while the pre-project situation still exists; once the new system is running, the reference point against which change would be measured no longer exists
options.B: Because the framework has to be reproduced verbatim in the vendor's technical bid
options.C: Because indicators cannot be revised at all once a project has commenced
options.D: Because monitoring reports must be submitted before a project can be sanctioned

questions.explanation: Building the framework early is what makes measurement of change possible at all — the pre-intervention values of waiting time, number of visits, cost of access and error rates cannot be recovered retrospectively once the manual process has been replaced. Indicators can and often should be refined during implementation; what cannot be recreated later is the baseline.

questions.question: Which of the following is an outcome indicator for a project computerising the issue of revenue certificates?

options.A: Number of desktop computers installed in tehsil offices
options.B: Average number of days taken to issue a certificate from the date of application
options.C: Number of officials trained on the new application
options.D: Amount of project budget released to the implementing agency

questions.explanation: Turnaround time measures the change in the service the citizen actually receives, which is what an outcome indicator is for. Computers installed and officials trained are outputs of the project's activities, and budget released is an input — all three can look healthy while certificates still take as long as they did before.

questions.question: An M&E team proposes an indicator for which no routine data is collected anywhere and for which no survey has been budgeted. Why should the indicator be replaced?

options.A: Because performance indicators must always be expressed in financial terms
options.B: Because an indicator not named in the Detailed Project Report cannot be used
options.C: Because an indicator with no feasible and affordable means of measurement will simply never be reported, leaving the objective it was meant to track invisible
options.D: Because outcome indicators are not permitted in a monitoring framework

questions.explanation: Measurability is a defining property of a usable indicator: if collecting the data is impractical or unfunded, the cell in the report stays empty and the objective goes unmonitored. The right response is to substitute a measurable proxy drawn from data the system or the department already generates, not to keep an unmeasurable indicator on paper.

questions.question: What is a baseline in a monitoring and evaluation framework?

options.A: The value of each indicator measured before the intervention begins, which serves as the reference point against which later change is assessed
options.B: The minimum performance level below which penalties become payable by the implementing vendor
options.C: The value of each indicator that the project commits to reach by its completion date
options.D: The average value of the indicator observed across comparable states

questions.explanation: The baseline fixes the 'before' picture, so that any later reading of the same indicator, measured the same way, expresses a change rather than a bare number. Option C describes the target, which is the intended end value; a baseline and a target are two ends of the same measurement and neither is meaningful without the other.

questions.question: A completed project reports that revenue certificates are now issued in seven days on average. No measurement of issue time was taken before the project began. What can legitimately be claimed?

options.A: That the project reduced issue time, because seven days is obviously faster than manual processing
options.B: That the project met its target, since seven days falls within the prescribed norm
options.C: That the extent of improvement can be reconstructed from the vendor's service level reports
options.D: Only that the current issue time is seven days; with no baseline, no improvement can be quantified or attributed to the project

questions.explanation: Attribution requires a comparison, and without a pre-project measurement there is nothing to compare seven days against — the claim of improvement rests on assumption, not evidence. Vendor service level reports only cover the period after go-live and describe the vendor's compliance with the contract, so they cannot supply the missing 'before' value.

questions.question: In the logical framework matrix, which column records the external conditions outside the project's control that must hold if results at one level are to lead to results at the next?
questions.explanation: The assumptions column makes the project's causal logic honest by naming what it is relying on but cannot deliver — continued power and connectivity, timely amendment of rules, staff remaining in post — each of which becomes a risk if it fails. Indicators say how achievement will be measured and means of verification say where that evidence comes from; neither captures external dependencies.

questions.question: What does the 'means of verification' column of a logical framework specify?

options.A: The officer accountable for achieving each objective
options.B: The budget allocated to each activity in the project
options.C: The source and method by which the evidence for each indicator will be obtained, such as a departmental MIS report, an audit record or a citizen survey
options.D: The external conditions assumed to remain favourable during implementation

questions.explanation: Means of verification ties every indicator to a named, obtainable piece of evidence, which is what stops the matrix from listing indicators that nobody can actually produce a number for. Naming the evidence source at design time also exposes indicators whose verification would cost more than the information is worth.
